summary: Supply the emitted frequency, the wave velocity, the receiver velocity and the source velocity and the Doppler effect calculator solves for observed frequency (f). It suits a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Doppler effect calculator work?
sections.html:
The Doppler effect calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports observed frequency (f) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the emitted frequency (f₀), the wave velocity (v), the receiver velocity (vr) and the source velocity (vₛ).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Doppler effect calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Observed frequency (f)=emitted frequency (f₀) × (wave velocity (v) + receiver velocity (vr)) ÷ (wave velocity (v) + source velocity (vₛ))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Emitted frequency (f₀) = 10 Hz, Wave velocity (v) = 10 m/s, Receiver velocity (vr) = 10 m/s and Source velocity (vₛ) = 10 m/s. The calculator returns Observed frequency (f) = 10 Hz.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Observed frequency (f) = 10 Hz should be roughly the size you expected from Emitted frequency (f₀) = 10 Hz and Wave velocity (v) = 10 m/s.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in hertz, and convertible to any of the 21 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Frequency, opening in hertz
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Frequency, opening in hertz

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Doppler effect calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the emitted frequency, the wave velocity and the receiver velocity — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Doppler effect calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns observed frequency (f), derived from the emitted frequency, the wave velocity and the receiver velocity. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Doppler effect calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the emitted frequency, the wave velocity, the receiver velocity and the source velocity, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter emitted frequency (f₀) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Emitted frequency (f₀) opens in hertz and the chip beside it offers 21 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Observed frequency (f) = 10 Hz. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Doppler effect calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
